text.p: Coca-Cola Enterprises Inc. reported a smaller-than-expected first-quarter loss Tuesday, sending the bottler's stock higher.
The Atlanta-based bottler of Coke products reported a loss of $33,000, or 27 cents a share, including a 3 cents per share one-time charge for the redemption of long-term debt.

Although the result compared with a profit of $5,000, or 4 cents per share, a year earlier, it came in well ahead of expectations on Wall Street, where the consensus expectation was for a quarterly loss of 30 cents a share, according to First Call, which tracks estimates.
Revenues rose to $2.1 billion from $1.60 billion a year earlier.
"The results were extremely good," said UBS Securities analyst Anton Brenner.
Coke Enterprises' stock climbed $1.875, or 3 percent, to $57.50 on the New York Stock Exchange as at least two analysts raised their earnings estimates for 1997.

Among the strongest indicators in the Coke Enterprises results was a 9 percent jump in U.S. case volumes, its best quarterly volume increase in the domestic market since 1988. Meanwhile, European volumes increased 14 percent for the company, in which Coca-Cola has a 44 percent stake.
Analysts said the U.S. volume rise came despite extreme competition and predicted the pace would be sustained.

They also expressed enthusiasm for the company's coming performance this year in Europe, where it has spent $2.92 billion to purchase Coke bottling operations in Belgium, France and Britain within the past eight months.
In 1996, the European soft-drink market was softened by bad weather late in the year.

"We've got an indication of how much leverage they could have outside this country, in terms of developing accelerating volume trends in Europe in particular," said Prudential Securities' George Thompson.

In February, Coke Enteprises bought U.K. bottler Coca-Cola and Schweppes Beverages Ltd. from joint owners Coca-Cola and Cadbury-Schweppes for $2 billion. Last July, it purchased Coca-Cola bottling operations in Belgium and France for $915 million.
